title: Universal Camera Corp. v. NLRB
lead: An examiner and the NLRB disagree about a discharge, and judicial review turns on what weight the examiner’s contrary account retains.

actors.name: National Labor Relations Board
actors.role: Agency defending reinstatement, back pay, and a cease-and-desist order.

actors.name: Discharged employee
actors.role: Beneficiary of the Board’s order, who had testified in an earlier Board proceeding.

actors.name: Trial examiner
actors.role: Administrative factfinder who heard the witnesses and recommended dismissal.

proceedings: The examiner recommended dismissal; the Board rejected that recommendation and ordered relief.
The Second Circuit enforced over Judge Swan’s dissent.
The Supreme Court vacated and remanded for whole-record review giving the examiner’s report its proper significance.
limits: The Supreme Court did not decide the true reason for the discharge or direct a final enforcement outcome. Casebook factual detail and subsequent appellate history are identified as editorial rather than new Supreme Court findings.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An employee’s earlier testimony precedes a disputed discharge
sections.cue: What competing explanations reached the agency?
paragraphs: Universal Camera Corporation employed a worker who testified in an earlier National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) proceeding and was later discharged. The parties disputed the reason for the discharge. The assigned casebook introduction adds that he was a supervisor who testified at a representation hearing about maintenance employees; the employer attributed discharge to his refusal to discipline another worker. The employee pointed to a nearly month-long delay after that incident and an earlier accusation of perjury by the dismissing officer. Those details come from the editorial introduction, not new factual determinations by the Supreme Court.

The trial examiner heard the witnesses, accepted the company’s account, and recommended dismissing the unfair-labor-practice proceeding. The Board disagreed. Finding protected testimony had caused the discharge, it ordered reinstatement and back pay and directed the company to stop discrimination against employees for filing charges or testifying under the National Labor Relations Act.

sources.pinpoint: Parties; Material Facts; 340 U.S. at 476,491–496; casebook 913

sections.title: The Second Circuit enforces without counting the disagreement with the examiner
sections.cue: Why did the reviewing method become the issue?
paragraphs: The company challenged enforcement. The Second Circuit enforced the Board’s order over Judge Swan’s dissent. It treated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) of 1946 and labor-law amendments of 1947 as leaving the judicial review function materially unchanged, and concluded that the Board’s disagreement with its examiner could not itself count against the substituted findings.

The Supreme Court granted review amid disagreement among circuits and considered the issue alongside the distinct Pittsburgh Steamship case. Universal Camera asked whether the whole record included both contrary evidence and the examiner’s rejected findings, and whether the evidence already required refusing enforcement. The companion proceeding was not another stage of this company’s case.

sections.title: Frankfurter explains why the whole record changes the inquiry
sections.cue: Does substantial evidence allow the court to retry the facts?
paragraphs: Justice Frankfurter traced reform of a review practice sometimes reduced to finding adequate support somewhere in the record. Criticism of the Board influenced legislation, but he declined to endorse every accusation, some of which were reckless or unfounded. The Attorney General’s Committee, the APA, and Taft-Hartley history reflected both continuity in the substantial-evidence formula and dissatisfaction with its application. More intrusive weight-of-the-evidence proposals did not become law.

Substantial evidence means relevant evidence a reasonable mind could accept as adequate, more than a scintilla. Its strength must be measured against everything that fairly detracts from the finding. The labor statute and APA called for the same approach in this record-based fact-review setting. That did not erase other statutory review categories for other agency actions.

Agencies retained their specialized responsibility, and courts could not replace a choice between two fairly conflicting views merely because they preferred the other. But favorable testimony did not compel enforcement if the full record prevented conscientious acceptance of the evidence as substantial. Application required judgment rather than a numerical formula.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning; Rule and Holding; 340 U.S. at 477–490 & n.15

sections.title: The Board’s power to disagree does not erase the examiner’s report
sections.cue: Why is neither clear-error review nor irrelevance correct?
paragraphs: The Second Circuit treated significance for the examiner’s findings as equivalent to giving them the binding status of a master’s findings. The Supreme Court rejected that choice. Final administrative authority belonged to the Board, and the APA gave it the powers it would possess as initial decisionmaker. It therefore need not find the examiner clearly erroneous before rejecting his view.

The APA nevertheless included initial and recommended decisions in the record and sought more independent, competent examiners. An experienced examiner’s opportunity to observe witnesses could reduce the apparent strength of evidence supporting a contrary Board result. The report deserved the significance it reasonably had in the particular case, including the role of credibility, consistency, and inherent probability. Demeanor-based disagreement could matter differently from competing inferences from undisputed documents, without imposing a rigid hierarchy or changing the substantial-evidence standard.

The Board’s preponderance obligation under § 10(c), a court’s substantial-evidence review, and the rejected clearly-erroneous limitation on Board review operated at different stages. They were not interchangeable tests.

sections.title: The Supreme Court leaves either enforcement outcome available
sections.cue: What did the existing record establish, and who disagreed?
paragraphs: The Second Circuit had in fact considered conflicting evidence, so disagreement with its description of the legislation did not alone demand reversal. Inconsistent company testimony and evidence that the dismissing officer had previously reacted against the employee’s Board appearance made enforcement permissible. The Supreme Court refused to hold that the company necessarily won on evidentiary sufficiency. Ordinary application belonged primarily to the courts of appeals, with Supreme Court intervention for rare misunderstanding or gross misapplication.

Black and Douglas joined Parts I and II but agreed with the lower court as to Part III’s examiner-report issue. They supplied no developed separate explanation, so none should be invented. Judge Swan’s lower-court dissent and disagreement among Attorney General’s Committee members were separate matters, not their Supreme Court reasoning.

The Court vacated and remanded to the Second Circuit to give the examiner’s report its proper evidentiary significance and reconsider the case more generally if appropriate. It allowed either enforcement or nonenforcement, without declaring the discharge lawful or finally directing reinstatement. The casebook reports a later refusal of enforcement and stronger language about credibility findings; that is subsequent appellate history, not the Supreme Court’s open-ended remand.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment; Separate Opinions; Notes; 340 U.S. at 490–492,497; casebook 918–919
